claims.text: The as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy has an abrupt, hysteretic magnetocaloric response.
Residual intrinsic stresses and microstructural defects primarily govern the hysteretic magnetocaloric response by pinning the magnetostructural phase front.
The as-deposited alloy is in an ordered, single-phase hexagonal state.
The as-deposited alloy contains inherent residual stresses and microstructural heterogeneities.
A suitably controlled sub-transition-temperature anneal can relieve residual stress without causing phase decomposition or significant grain coarsening.
Dislocations and grain-boundary configurations can pin the magnetostructural interface.
Relaxing intrinsic stress reduces the energy barrier for the magnetostructural transition.
A reduced transition barrier permits a broader and more gradual phase transformation with less kinetic hindrance.
Reduced phase-boundary pinning lowers hysteresis while preserving a significant entropy change.
Annealed samples will have a smoother magnetocaloric entropy-change profile than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed samples will have a smaller hysteresis width than the as-deposited baseline under identical low-field cycling conditions.
Annealed samples will exhibit improved effective heat-exchange rates under identical low-field cycling conditions.
The as-deposited baseline undergoes a sharp, first-order magnetostructural transition with pronounced hysteresis.
The baseline has limited heat exchange because of a low surface-to-volume ratio.
The predictions apply to the non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi composition in thin-film or similar geometries under low applied magnetic fields.
Substantially different microstructures or compositions may change the predicted outcome.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as having a low surface-to-volume ratio that limits heat exchange, whereas the stated prediction domain is thin-film or similar geometry, which ordinarily represents the geometry selected to provide a comparatively high surface-to-volume ratio.

Improved heat-exchange rate is predicted after annealing even though the proposed intervention does not change geometry and the baseline attributes limited heat exchange to surface-to-volume ratio. The stated stress-relaxation mechanism therefore does not account for this predicted thermal-rate improvement.
